newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Yorks Water sees steady '97 growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Yorks Water sees steady '97 growth.

text.p: British water and sewerage company Yorkshire Water Plc on Friday said it looked forward to steady growth in 1997 as increased efficiency brought improved customer service and better shareholder value, but it could not say how the new Labour government's planned windfall tax would affect the group.
"The business is sound. It is each and every year becoming more efficient," group chief executive Kevin Bond told Reuters in an interview.
But a cloud of uncertainty still looms for all Britain's privatised utilities with the arrival of Tony Blair's Labour regime.
And, Bond said, the effect on Yorkshire Water of Labour's windfall tax would remain unclear until full details were given.
"We are waiting to hear what the new government will say," he added.

Yorkshire Water had done a great deal to overcome the difficulties which saw it unable to secure and deliver water, most notoriously in the summer drought of 1995, Bond said. His assurance came after the government issued this year's first drought order on Thursday.
"Our reservoirs are 87 percent full and that's across Yorkshire," said Bond. "We've re-engineered the system completely which puts us in a far stronger position."
The company was working to give shareholders "more bang for the buck" through improved efficiency and satisfying customers, he said.
Water customers have attacked utilities over water shortages which have forced the imposition of hosepipe bans and the installing of stand-pipes.
But while reservoir and river levels were healthy, Bond said Yorkshire could cope with the low aquifer levels which helped support east Yorkshire by using the developed grid network.
Yorkshire Water, which posted pre-tax profit of 162.2 million sterling in 1996, had implemented a 170 million stg investment programme since 1995.
The investment in an additional 240 kms of pipeline and 28 new pumping stations would enable vast quantities of water to be moved around Yorkshire.
By investing a further 20 million sterling each year in additional leakage reduction, Yorkshire Water would steadily improve efficiency.

The investment had already brought leakage down to 328 megalitres a day from 435 megalitres in 1995, enough to supply daily a town the size of Huddersfield, which has a population of 120,000, Bond said.
